summary:
Saskatchewan operates inside Canada's national legal framework. Federal law, federal documents and federal agencies are carried by the national assessment; the findings below concern matters that arise under provincial law.

Saskatchewan's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, which gives a visitor or resident a provincial complaints route.

Change of legal gender is a provincial function and is available in Saskatchewan under the province's own rules.

In August 2023 the education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies: schools must seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of a student under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. The measure was enacted as The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023, passed with the Charter's notwithstanding clause invoked as a five-year override.

The Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan, in Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74 on 11 August 2025, set aside the 2023 chambers decision on the policy. Invocation of the notwithstanding clause prevents the consent rule from being struck down, but the court held that a judge retains jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights and to issue a declaration to that effect. UR Pride's challenge continues in the Court of King's Bench.

Amnesty International Canada, which intervened in the appeal, welcomed the ruling as a meaningful victory for the protection of human rights and argued that use of the override clause must be consistent with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy.

On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear appeals from both the provincial government and UR Pride, expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. No decision on the merits has changed the consent policy, which has applied to schools since 2023; Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen noted at the time of the appellate ruling that students had been living under the law for two years.

Saskatchewan grants parental status to three or more intentional parents, one of three provinces to do so alongside British Columbia and Ontario, extending recognition to a wider range of queer and trans families.
tangentialFactors:
Reporting on the 11 August 2025 appellate ruling divides over how much jurisdiction the courts retain. One account treats the decision as a holding that courts cannot examine whether the policy breaches the Charter's equality and limitations provisions once the override applies; others read it as confirming jurisdiction to assess whether the law limits Charter rights and to issue a declaration, while barring invalidation. The reasons in 2025 SKCA 74 are the controlling text.

The Supreme Court of Canada has grouped the Saskatchewan appeal with the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21, bringing two provincial uses of the constitutional override before the court in the same expedited proceeding.
localsOnly:
Students under 16 in Saskatchewan schools need parent or guardian permission before a preferred name or pronouns are changed at school. Parents are to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party programs in schools were paused when the policy was announced in August 2023.

Legal change of gender for Saskatchewan residents is processed under provincial rules rather than federal ones.

Saskatchewan recognises three or more intentional parents, one of three provinces to do so, and same-sex couples have been able to adopt in the province since 2001.
outOfScopeNotes:
Saskatchewan's specific requirements for amending a gender marker on provincial documents, including which evidence is required and which documents can be changed, are not documented in the available sources.

No Saskatchewan-specific provincial correctional policy or case on housing prisoners by gender identity is documented; custodial placement in federal institutions is a national matter and sits with the national assessment.

The constitutional question is unresolved. The Supreme Court of Canada has granted a hearing, no merits decision has been issued, and the override invoked with the 2023 amendment runs for five years.

Sources describe the conduct that triggers the school consent requirement in differing terms, as a change of name or pronouns and as use of a gender-related preferred name or gender identity; the wording of the Act itself is the authority.
